metadata.title: Trends in mathematics motivation between 1980 and 2015: Exploring the educational-gender-equality paradox over time

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS/SIMS student questionnaire data to construct country-level (system-level) gender gaps in intrinsic and extrinsic mathematics motivation, and also constructs achievement gaps using linked achievement scales. For aggregating the five plausible motivation scores per student to system-level means, the authors explicitly state that the means are weighted with senate weights that sum to 500 for each country’s data, and that Rubin’s (1987) rules/multiple imputation are used to pool across plausible responses. The paper does not report the use of student-level sampling/survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or any replicate-weight scheme; instead, it focuses on senate-weighted aggregation for country means and fixed-effects panel modeling at the country-year level. Because the analysis is panel regression on aggregated gaps (not ML training), the manuscript does not discuss applying complex survey weights to regression estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses three TIMSS/SIMS time points: SIMS 1980 (ages 13–15; grade 8 in most systems, with some grade 7/9 systems), TIMSS 1995 (eighth-grade systems), and TIMSS 2015 (eighth-grade systems). It constructs two country panels based on overlap of participating systems: Panel A uses 11 educational systems common to SIMS 1980 and TIMSS 1995 (Belgium (French), England, France, Hong Kong (grade 7), Hungary, Israel, Netherlands, New Zealand, Sweden (grade 7), Thailand, United States), and Panel B uses 18 systems common to TIMSS 1995 and 2015 (Australia, Canada, England, Hong Kong (grade 8), Hungary, Iran, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Republic of Korea, Lithuania, New Zealand, Russian Federation, Singapore, Slovenia, Sweden (grade 8), Thailand, United States). For missing data in motivation items due to questionnaire changes, the authors fit country-specific IRT measurement models and generate five plausible sum scores per person per construct, then pool to system-level means using Rubin’s rules. For parental education subgroup analyses, they exclude England entirely because it contains all missing values on both parental education variables, and they exclude 4.41% of the original sample in SIMS who only used the middle response option on the motivation questionnaires.

main_findings.dataset_used: SIMS 1980 & TIMSS 1995 (Panel A), grade 8/7 systems, mathematics motivation (intrinsic) gender gap
main_findings.target_variable: Intrinsic motivation gender gap change (boys minus girls)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Panel regression (two-way fixed effects, robust SE clustered by country). Model 1 (ST95, n=11): HDI estimate -3.905 (SE 1.439), t=-2.713, p=.024, R2=.358; lower parental education: HDI -4.057 (SE 1.286), t=-3.155, p=.014, R2=.450; higher parental education: HDI -2.719 (SE 2.885), t=-0.943, p=.373, R2=.091. Model 2 (ST95, n=11): HDI -4.209 (SE 1.144), t=-3.681, p=.006, R2=.565; lower: HDI -1.396 (SE 0.441), t=-3.169, p=.013, R2=.557; higher: HDI -3.018 (SE 2.227), t=-1.355, p=.218, R2=.339.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using SIMS 1980 & TIMSS 1995 (Panel A) the study leveraged Human Development Index (HDI), the mathematics achievement gender gap, and parental education subgrouping to model the change in the intrinsic motivation gender gap (boys minus girls), finding that higher HDI significantly predicted a more negative intrinsic motivation gap from 1980 to 1995 (i.e., boys’ intrinsic motivation advantage over girls increased), but only for students with lower-than-median parental education. This indicates that the educational-gender-equality paradox for intrinsic mathematics motivation is concentrated among students from less-educated families, suggesting targeted motivation-support policies for disadvantaged groups in more developed contexts, while causality is limited by the panel assumptions and aggregation level.

main_findings.dataset_used: SIMS 1980 & TIMSS 1995 (Panel A), grade 8/7 systems, mathematics motivation (intrinsic) gender gap
main_findings.target_variable: Intrinsic motivation gender gap change (boys minus girls) — GDP sensitivity
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using SIMS 1980 & TIMSS 1995 (Panel A) the study leveraged log GDP per capita, the mathematics achievement gender gap, and parental education subgrouping to model the change in the intrinsic motivation gender gap, finding that GDP showed limited and subgroup-sensitive associations (notably a marginally significant negative GDP effect in the higher parental-education group in Model 5, but not robustly after adding the achievement gap in Model 6). This indicates that economic development measured via GDP alone does not fully replicate the HDI pattern, suggesting that broader human-development components (education and life expectancy alongside income) may be more informative for understanding motivation-gap dynamics.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 1995 & TIMSS 2015 (Panel B), grade 8 systems, mathematics motivation (intrinsic) gender gap
main_findings.target_variable: Intrinsic motivation gender gap change (boys minus girls)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 1995 & TIMSS 2015 (Panel B) the study leveraged Human Development Index (HDI), the mathematics achievement gender gap, and parental education subgrouping to model the change in the intrinsic motivation gender gap (boys minus girls), finding no statistically significant relationship between HDI and the intrinsic motivation gap change from 1995 to 2015 in either panel or parental-education subgroup. This indicates that the educational-gender-equality paradox for intrinsic motivation does not persist uniformly across later decades, implying that policy attention may need to be time-sensitive and focused on earlier periods or specific disadvantaged subgroups rather than assuming a stable development–motivation pattern.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 1995 & TIMSS 2015 (Panel B), grade 8 systems, mathematics motivation (intrinsic) gender gap
main_findings.target_variable: Intrinsic motivation gender gap change (boys minus girls) — GDP sensitivity
main_findings.performance_metrics: Panel regression (two-way fixed effects, robust SE clustered by country). Model 5 (T95T15, n=18): GDP -0.143 (SE 0.063), t=-2.267, p=.038, R2=.261; lower: GDP -0.246 (SE 0.065), t=-3.775, p=.002, R2=.435; higher: GDP 0.012 (SE 0.095), t=0.125, p=.902, R2=.001. Model 6 (T95T15, n=18): GDP -0.129 (SE 0.063), t=-2.019, p=.061, R2=.398; lower: GDP -0.257 (SE 0.061), t=-4.222, p<.001, R2=.572; higher: GDP 0.010 (SE 0.097), t=0.098, p=.923, R2=.003; achievement gap included with GDP.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 1995 & TIMSS 2015 (Panel B) the study leveraged log GDP per capita, the mathematics achievement gender gap, and parental education subgrouping to model the change in the intrinsic motivation gender gap, finding that GDP significantly predicted a decrease in the intrinsic motivation gender gap (i.e., reduced boys’ advantage over girls) from 1995 to 2015, primarily for students with lower-than-median parental education. This indicates that economic growth may be associated with narrowing intrinsic motivation gender gaps for disadvantaged students in later decades, supporting policies that combine development-oriented investments with targeted equity measures.

main_findings.dataset_used: SIMS 1980 & TIMSS 1995 (Panel A), grade 8/7 systems, mathematics motivation (extrinsic) gender gap
main_findings.target_variable: Extrinsic motivation gender gap change (boys minus girls)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Panel regression (two-way fixed effects, robust SE clustered by country). Model 3 (ST95, n=11): HDI -1.250 (SE 1.511), t=-0.827, p=.430, R2=.041; lower: HDI -0.230 (SE 1.324), t=-0.174, p=.867, R2=.001; higher: HDI 0.027 (SE 1.743), t=0.016, p=.988, R2<.001. Model 4 (ST95, n=11): HDI -1.395 (SE 1.389), t=-1.004, p=.345, R2=.094; lower: HDI 0.261 (SE 1.298), t=0.201, p=.846, R2=.002; higher: HDI -0.112 (SE 1.600), t=-0.070, p=.946, R2=.092; achievement gap included.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using SIMS 1980 & TIMSS 1995 (Panel A) the study leveraged Human Development Index (HDI), the mathematics achievement gender gap, and parental education subgrouping to model the change in the extrinsic motivation gender gap, finding no statistically significant effect of HDI on extrinsic motivation gap change in either panel or parental-education subgroup. This indicates that the development–gender-equality paradox is not evident for extrinsic mathematics motivation over this earlier period, implying that interventions aimed at extrinsic motivation may require mechanisms beyond macro-level development and may instead depend on education-system practices.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 1995 & TIMSS 2015 (Panel B), grade 8 systems, mathematics motivation (extrinsic) gender gap
main_findings.target_variable: Extrinsic motivation gender gap change (boys minus girls)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Panel regression (two-way fixed effects, robust SE clustered by country). Model 3 (T95T15, n=18): HDI -0.271 (SE 0.666), t=-0.406, p=.690, R2=.007; lower: HDI 0.022 (SE 0.732), t=0.030, p=.976, R2=.006; higher: HDI -0.273 (SE 0.703), t=-0.388, p=.703, R2=.006. Model 4 (T95T15, n=18): HDI -0.433 (SE 0.638), t=-0.679, p=.507, R2=.035; lower: HDI -0.392 (SE 0.674), t=-0.582, p=.570, R2=.076; higher: HDI -0.272 (SE 0.752), t=-0.362, p=.723, R2=.006; achievement gap included.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 1995 & TIMSS 2015 (Panel B) the study leveraged Human Development Index (HDI), the mathematics achievement gender gap, and parental education subgrouping to model the change in the extrinsic motivation gender gap, finding no statistically significant relationship between HDI and extrinsic motivation gap change from 1995 to 2015 in either panel or parental-education subgroup. This indicates that extrinsic motivation gender gaps appear to evolve independently of macro-level development indices in this period, suggesting that system-level curriculum, assessment, and school-level motivational practices may be more relevant than national development for extrinsic motivation equity.

data.outcome_summary: The study investigates the educational-gender-equality paradox in mathematics motivation using longitudinal, system-level panel data built from SIMS 1980, TIMSS 1995, and TIMSS 2015. It constructs cross-culturally comparable intrinsic and extrinsic motivation scales via a market-basket approach and country-specific IRT measurement, generating five plausible sum scores per student and pooling to country means using Rubin’s rules; missing parental education data lead to excluding England from subgroup analyses. The main results come from two-way fixed-effects panel regressions (robust SE clustered by country) on country-level gender gaps. For intrinsic motivation, HDI significantly predicts changes from 1980 to 1995 (notably for students with lower-than-median parental education), while HDI shows no effect from 1995 to 2015; GDP shows a significant narrowing pattern from 1995 to 2015 for the lower parental-education group. For extrinsic motivation, neither HDI nor GDP significantly predicts gender-gap change in either panel. Limitations include aggregation to country-level gaps, subgroup analyses with substantial missingness, and the fact that the paper uses causal language despite relying on observational panel assumptions rather than randomized identification.
